#9864. Grabette: an open system to record robot-manipulation data

Record your own manipulation tasks in minutes with a handheld gripper, turn them into robot-ready datasets automatically, and help grow an open, collaborative dataset for robot learning.

Robot learning has a supply problem. We have capable policy architectures (transformer-based VLAs, diffusion and flow-matching policies, and even world models) and the GPUs to train them. What we lack is large, diverse, real-world manipulation data.

Teleoperating a robot to collect it can be expensive and demanding: first of all, it requires a robot. And depending on the teleoperation method, data collection can be tedious for the user if it takes hours and involve significant hardware and logistical challenges. That is difficult to scale with the wide variety of tasks and environnements required.

But you don't need a robot to collect robot data. Just a human hand, a gripper, a camera, and a way to recover the 6-DoF trajectory of what the hand did. Capture the demonstration and you have data a robot can learn from.

That's what we're releasing today: Grabette, an open, low-cost system for recording manipulation data. Pick it up, record a task with your own hand, and get back a clean, robot-ready dataset. No robot, no lab, no teleop rig.

And that's the bigger goal: if recording a demonstration is as easy as shooting a video, anyone can contribute. We want Grabette to seed a large, open, collaborative manipulation dataset. One no single lab could ever build alone.

Grabette is directly inspired by the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) from Stanford: a handheld gripper with a fisheye camera that records demonstrations "in the wild", recovers camera trajectories with SLAM, and trains visuomotor policies from them.

UMI proved the recipe works. Other (closed source) devices exists like Agibot's MEgo gripper, Genrobot's DAS gripper and Sunday Robotics skill capture glove. Our goal was to make it effortless to use, to get the barrier from "I have a task" to "I have a trained model" as low as possible.

Grabette is built into the modern open ecosystem: LeRobot for datasets, the Hugging Face Hub for sharing, and a processing pipeline you run from your browser with nothing to install. Grabette is something anyone can build on a workbench, use in the field, and contribute data from.

We have been developing Grabette for months, and we feel it has become usable enough to share. We are excited to share it now with you!

Grabette is a handheld gripper instrumented with everything needed to reconstruct a manipulation demonstration.

It carries two cameras, each with a distinct job. Splitting the two roles is deliberate: the cheap wide fisheye gives the policy the context-rich, wrist-camera-style view it needs, while the RGBD camera does the heavy lifting of robust 6-DoF tracking.

And while Grabette records data during tasks performed by a user, it relies on its robotic counterpart to execute the movements it has learned after training. So, meet Gripette, the robotic arm end-effector twin of Grabette.

Grabette hand held recording device (left) and Gripette robot gripper (right)

Components. Standard sensors you can buy, no closed pipeline, no fork lock-in. A Raspberry Pi, a standard Pi camera, an off-the-shelf OAK-D depth camera, magnetic encoders. The whole point is that anyone can build one from parts you can just order.

Robot-agnostic by design. Nothing in the capture or the data format assumes a particular arm. Demonstrations are stored as camera-local 6-DoF cartesian pose plus gripper state, the output is a standard LeRobot dataset on the Hugging Face Hub, so the same data can drive different robots and different learning methods. You will still need the matching Gripette gripper on your arm though.

This release enables anyone to go from "I want to demonstrate a task" to "I have a training-ready dataset" quickly and without prior expertise.

Press the button, and data from the observation camera, the tracking camera (color, depth, and IMU), and the gripper’s encoder joint values are recorded simultaneously, using a single shared clock to ensure proper synchronization. Press the button again to stop the episode, and the data is saved locally on the Raspberry Pi.

Open the Grabette dashboard in your browser. Select the episodes you want to add to the dataset, and with one click, post-processing begins.

Everything is now ready to start training!

A dataset is only interesting if it trains something. So, to show the loop end-to-end, we ship a complete example. But to be clear, this is an example of what is enables, not the product: the release is the recording system. Your Grabette data works with any method that consumes LeRobot datasets.

Our example takes 200 recorded demonstrations such as :

The data bottleneck doesn’t get solved by one lab, but by a community recording demonstrations everywhere. You can now help build the dataset: build a Grabette, record tasks you are interested in, and share them on the Hub. Every episode makes the open dataset bigger and more diverse, and every contributor makes robot learning a little less gated behind expensive hardware.

This release is only the start of the project! Grabette will keep evolving. We already have more coming, including Casquette, a head-mounted POV device to complement Grabette for egocentric capture (still a work in progress). But the most important next step isn’t only ours, it’s also yours: start recording, and let’s build the dataset together.

👉 Build a Grabette (GitHub) · Process your data (HF Space) · Contribute to the dataset

#9863. NASA Mars rover and orbiter suffer glitches

It isn't only systems on Earth suffering technical problems

It's been a bad few weeks for technology on and off the planet, as NASA reported problems with its Perseverance Mars rover and Odyssey orbiter this week.

For Perseverance, the problem seems to be a relatively straightforward communications issue that has paused science operations because of low data rates. The Odyssey orbiter, however, is facing an issue that could end the mission.

The 2001 Mars Odyssey reached orbit around Mars in October 2001 to search for evidence of water and ice on the surface. The mission was supposed to last two and a half years, but the spacecraft's operations have been extended for a quarter of a century.

In that time, it has had its fair share of ups and downs, including the failure of one of its four reaction wheels in 2013. Three reaction wheels are needed to orient the spacecraft; otherwise, it must fall back to its hydrazine thrusters.

Earlier in November, between the 4th and 6th, Odyssey dropped into safe mode, which engineers determined was caused by one of the remaining reaction wheels stopping spinning. Science data stopped flowing as the team worked to recover the component; the good news was that the wheel moved when commanded. The bad news is that if the thrusters need to be used, only a few months of fuel remain.

More bad news is that the spacecraft is part of NASA's Mars Relay Network, and was responsible for sending back the first post-landing images from the Phoenix lander and the Spirit, Opportunity, and Curiosity rovers. Its loss (should it come to that) would therefore be keenly felt.

In the event the orbiter is indeed approaching the end of the road, the European Space Agency's Mars Express (MEX) and Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) could pick up some of the load although, as a former ESA insider put it: "MEX is a science mission that can do relay where TGO is a relay mission that also does science." According to NASA, TGO already sends the most relay data from Mars to Earth.

The challenge facing the Perseverance trundlebot is one of communication. On October 30, the rover's main computer detected problems with the primary radio (a series of "heartbeats" from the device did not arrive as expected) and automatically switched to a redundant backup, placing itself in a protective safe mode.

So far, so expected. Engineers brought the rover back from safe mode, analyzed the data, and made an unpleasant discovery. The backup radio was not performing as it should – it was operating at approximately half of its expected power output.

Both radios were therefore deemed inoperable – at least until the team has got to the bottom of the issues – and the rover has used X-band communications over its high-gain antenna to talk to Earth ever since. The problem here is that the connection provides a significantly lower data rate, meaning science and instrument operations are on hold.

Engineers are working first to return the backup radio to operational status, then to address the primary. ®

#9862. Bringing Nunchaku 4-bit Diffusion Inference to Diffusers

Large diffusion transformers can create stunning images (or even videos, audio snippets, and now text), but loading a modern text-to-image model in BF16 precision often requires 20-30 GB of VRAM, which puts these models out of reach of most consumer GPUs. Quantization is a powerful solution to this problem, and Diffusers already integrates several quantization backends such as bitsandbytes, GGUF, torchao, and Quanto, which we covered in Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers.

Most of these backends are weight-only. This means that they store the weights in low precision and dequantize them back to high precision at compute time. This reduces memory usage significantly, but it usually does not make inference faster, and can even add a small latency overhead.

SVDQuant, the quantization method behind the popular Nunchaku inference engine, takes a different approach. It runs the main transformer layers with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4), reducing memory while also speeding up the denoising loop. The details are covered below, but until now, using these checkpoints required a separate inference library.

With current Diffusers, loading a Nunchaku checkpoint is as simple as calling from_pretrained(), with no local CUDA compilation required thanks to the kernels package. In addition, the companion diffuse-compressor toolkit lets you quantize new architectures yourself and publish them as regular Diffusers repositories.

First, install the requirements. You need a recent version of Diffusers and the Hugging Face kernels package:

Then load a pre-quantized pipeline like any other Diffusers model:

No custom pipeline class or separate inference engine is needed, and there is nothing to compile locally. The NVFP4 kernels are downloaded from the Hub through the Nunchaku Lite kernels page the first time they are used. This checkpoint pairs a Nunchaku NVFP4 transformer with a bitsandbytes NF4 text encoder, and generates a 1024x1024 image in about 1.7 seconds on an RTX 5090 with a peak memory usage of about 12 GB, compared with about 24 GB for the BF16 pipeline. You can find more details about the Nunchaku Lite checkpoint format in the official Diffusers documentation.

NVFP4 checkpoints require an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU (RTX 50 series, RTX PRO 6000, B200). For earlier generations, use the INT4 variants. See the hardware support table below for details.

SVDQuant is the quantization method behind Nunchaku, its reference CUDA inference engine. Standard 4-bit quantization is difficult for diffusion transformers because both weights and activations contain large outliers. SVDQuant handles this by moving activation outliers into the weights, representing the hardest part of each weight matrix with a small 16-bit low-rank branch, and quantizing the remaining residual to 4 bits. Nunchaku makes this fast with fused kernels for the 4-bit path and the low-rank branch.

The original Nunchaku engine gets much of its speed from model-specific fused execution paths, such as fused QKV projections and fused GELU/MLP kernels. Those optimizations are tied to each architecture's module layout and checkpoint format, so supporting a new model family usually requires model-specific integration work.

Nunchaku Lite is the new integration path in Diffusers. With it, Diffusers can load Nunchaku-style checkpoints without a custom pipeline or a separate inference engine. Under the hood, Nunchaku Lite patches the relevant nn.Linear modules of a stock Diffusers model with runtime SVDQ/AWQ linear layers before the checkpoint is loaded. The CUDA kernels come from the Hub through the kernels package. Two kernel families are used:

The trade-off is that, without architecture-specific fused kernels and modules, Nunchaku Lite cannot match the speedup of the original Nunchaku engine. However, the bare-bones implementation still delivers around 30% speedup while retaining the same level of VRAM reduction.

If you have used bitsandbytes or torchao in Diffusers, the mechanics will feel familiar. A Nunchaku Lite model repository is an ordinary Diffusers repository. The only special part is a quantization_config block inside the transformer's config.json:

This config tells Diffusers which modules were quantized, which scheme they use, and which Nunchaku Lite runtime layer to instantiate (SVDQW4A4Linear or AWQW4A16Linear).

Because the quantized model keeps the exact module structure of the dense one, everything downstream (schedulers, LoRA loading hooks, offloading, torch.compile) sees a normal Diffusers model.

Nunchaku Lite uses different kernel variants depending on the GPU generation and checkpoint precision:

Volta and Hopper GPUs are currently not supported by the 4-bit kernels. The quantizer validates the GPU's CUDA capability at load time and raises a clear error instead of producing incorrect outputs.

Nunchaku Lite can be combined with other Diffusers memory and speed optimizations.

torch.compile. Compiling the transformer improves the end-to-end speedup from 1.35x to 1.8x:

Quantized text encoders. The transformer is not the only component with a large memory footprint. Text encoders such as T5 or Qwen3 can occupy several gigabytes on their own. Further quantizing the text encoder with bitsandbytes NF4 reduces peak VRAM by about 22% in our benchmark.

Offloading. Diffusers offloading helpers such as enable_model_cpu_offload() and enable_sequential_cpu_offload() work as usual if you need to fit the pipeline onto a smaller GPU.

All numbers below were measured on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (Blackwell) at 1024x1024 using rootonchair/ERNIE-Image-Turbo-nunchaku-lite-int4-bnb4-text-encoder.

As shown above, Nunchaku reduces peak VRAM by up to 50% while still improving latency by roughly 30%. The remaining overhead comes largely from extra kernel launches, which torch.compile can mitigate, bringing the full pipeline down to 1.68 s, or 1.8x faster than the BF16 baseline.

Nunchaku Lite support in Diffusers is architecture-agnostic, and the diffuse-compressor toolkit provides an end-to-end SVDQuant workflow for Diffusers models: calibrate, quantize, package, and publish.

Below, we walk through quantizing FLUX.2 Klein 4B as an example. It covers the main steps: inspect the model, calibrate and quantize the transformer, package the result as a Diffusers pipeline, then verify and push it to the Hub. The full tutorial covers every flag in detail.

The generic scanner walks the model and decides what to target: compatible linears inside the repeated transformer-block stack become SVDQ W4A4 targets, recognized modulation linears become AWQ W4A16 targets, and everything else stays dense.

Always read this report before quantizing. For FLUX.2 Klein 4B, the expected result is 100 SVDQ targets, 3 AWQ targets, and 6 dense outer linears, with no missing patterns or duplicate names.

The following command runs SVDQuant on the transformer and writes the quantized checkpoint to outputs/checkpoints/svdq-int4_r32-flux-2-klein-4b.safetensors:

Replace --precision int4 with nvfp4 to build Blackwell-native weights.

The converter combines the quantized transformer with the base pipeline's other components, writes the compact nunchaku_lite configuration into transformer/config.json, and can optionally convert text encoders to NF4:

Once the outputs look good, run pipe.push_to_hub("your-name/your-model-nunchaku-lite-int4"). Other users can then load it with the same from_pretrained() pattern shown above.

Note that the generic path assumes the architecture can be quantized without structural rewrites. For additional speedup, the original Nunchaku engine rewrites groups of Diffusers layers as fused modules. The generic path cannot infer these changes on its own, such as combining separate Q, K, and V projections into one module or splitting a fused projection across several modules.

FLUX.1-dev's QKV projection is a concrete example. Diffusers defines three separate modules:

The Nunchaku FLUX module combines those layers into one quantized to_qkv module:

This grouped module is required because Nunchaku's fused operator consumes the QKV projection, Q/K normalization, and rotary embeddings together. By comparison, the default Diffusers path executes them separately:

The Nunchaku path supplies the grouped projection, normalization modules, and rotary embeddings to one fused operator:

This is the structural rewrite that the generic path cannot infer. Diffusers has three destination modules with to_q, to_k, and to_v parameter prefixes, while Nunchaku has one grouped module under to_qkv. A model-specific target config or adapter must state that the Q, K, and V parameters should be concatenated along the output dimension, in that order, and loaded into to_qkv.

Structural rewrites like these are described by a model-specific target config during quantization and handled by a small runtime adapter when the checkpoint is loaded. The FLUX.2 Klein 4B quantization script provides a concrete target-config example for producing a structurally rewritten checkpoint, while rootonchair/nunchaku-lite provides the runtime adapters needed to load grouped QKV tensors, split fused projections, and other fused operations. For the complete workflow, you can check the Adding A New Model guide.

To get started right away, check out the following repositories:

Nunchaku's SVDQuant kernels are one of the most effective ways to run diffusion transformers efficiently on consumer hardware, and they are now natively supported in Diffusers. Pre-quantized checkpoints load with from_pretrained(), and the diffuse-compressor toolkit makes it possible to quantize new architectures without waiting for engine support. By quantizing both weights and activations, the W4A4 path lowers memory use while improving denoising latency, keeping image quality close to the BF16 original.

If you quantize and publish a new model, we would love to hear about it. Share it on the Hub and let us know! If you have any questions about this feature, feel free to join our Discord.

To learn more, check out the following resources:

Thanks to the Diffusers maintainers for reviews and guidance throughout the integration, and to the MIT HAN Lab / Nunchaku team for the original SVDQuant work. Thanks to Marc Sun for providing feedback on the blog post. Thanks to Álvaro Somoza for trying out nunchaku-lite and for providing feedback.

rootonchair is also grateful to SilverAI for supporting this work and providing the environment in which much of this development took place.

#9860. ChatGPT shrunk down to run on a Super Nintendo

Just don't expect complex, coherent, or always correct answers

If you’ve ever wondered how small an instance of ChatGPT could get, wonder no longer. Someone has actually rigged up a tiny version of the chatbot to run on a Super Nintendo cartridge.

Tech journalist and retro tech enthusiast Benj Edwards is responsible for ChatGPT for SNES. He's published it online running in an emulator, complete with SNES-era music and sound effects, and for download as an SNES ROM, too.

It’s not a big model, mind you, and performance is thus pretty limited: According to the website, it’s a 2.2 million-parameter offshoot of OpenAI’s GPT-OSS-120b, which was used to develop its training conversations – so in that sense it truly is a ChatGPT that runs on an SNES cartridge. Edwards described it to The Register as a distilled version of the aforementioned open-weight model.

There are two options built into ChatGPT for SNES: One that’s purely the model, with every word generated coming right from its tiny little silicon brain, and another that includes a fact book culled from the opening sentences of around 150,000 simple English Wikipedia articles. If you opt to run both versions and ask it the same questions, you’ll notice a massive difference.

Given some of the other responses we got while testing, there’s really no good reason to run the base model – memory isn’t really an issue given the basic build is about 4MB and the factbook build is just 19MB.

Edwards admits that it’s not the most helpful AI model, either – this is just an experiment after all.

“It is not a useful assistant: the model is millions of times smaller than the models behind ChatGPT, knows about 8,000 words, and often gets things wrong, sometimes confidently,” Edwards noted in his writeup. In that sense, it really is vintage AI on vintage hardware. “The fact book can carry mistakes too.”

If you have an SNES lying around (lucky you), you can download the ROM from this link. If you want to get it running on an SNES you’ll need a cartridge that allows running of custom ROMs, and that supports Nintendo’s Super FX graphics coprocessor. Cartridges like the FXPak Pro and SD2SNES support it. The factbook version also requires support for the aftermarket Media Streaming Unit 1 (MSU-1), which adds CD-ROM like features to the SNES. MSU-1 is available in both of the flash carts mentioned above.

If you have some real hardware skills, however, you could technically make your own ChatGPT cartridge.

“The ‘pure’ version, which generates all responses from the AI language model, could run from a real custom SNES cart,” Edwards told us – it doesn’t even actually need the Super FX chip. “I do have a version of ChatGPT for SNES that can run without the Super FX chip, but without the extra processing power the answers are not as good.”

That said, Edwards believes its absolutely crazy and nonsensical answers are part of the fun.

“ChatGPT for SNES can definitely make mistakes too, but it's almost cute when it does it because of its limited knowledge and its playful interface,” Edwards told us.

While a human may have designed the experiment, the coding work was done by AI, Edwards told us – he’s been interested in it since the 1990s and is pursuing more experiments with tiny AI models using the help of the bigger ones.

“I've been theorizing about what I call ‘tiny talking machines’ … over the past year,” Edwards told us, and he’s been able to use coding agents to turn those ideas into actual software. ChatGPT for SNES is one example, and he also created an NES ROM called Séance that uses an even smaller AI model able to run on an original Nintendo Entertainment System that simulates talking to a ghost in a haunted game cartridge.

“I designed the scope of what the software should be, how it should work broadly, what chip it should use, how the interface should look and work, and the sounds it makes when it types responses,” Edwards told us. He added that he sees the project as an AI/human collaboration, which is where he believes AI works best.

“The AI agents who did the coding for this project currently advise that we've hit the limit of how good the AI model can be on the limited hardware,” Edwards said - he’s not taking their word for it, though. “It's up to human creativity to transcend those assumptions. I have already come up with new ideas that I believe can make a tiny model like ChatGPT for SNES even more coherent, and I'm working on them now.” ®

#9859. cgo's pointer check is all over the place

cgo does syntactic transformations unaware of Go types, allowing almost unnoticeable changes in source code to turn a 48ns call into a 76µs call. And its correctness checks can panic on legal code, while being exhaustive and expensive in some cases and lax in others.

In this article, we recap some of the basics of Go's Foreign Function Interface (FFI), cgo, and take a look at example programs that explain its behavior and limits. In particular we'll show how passing the same pointer to C can panic on code that the docs allow, how it can be about 1600x slower depending on how the C call is written, and when the cgo argument checker just gives up.Grab dependencies (clang, Go 1.27.0 and Go debugger, delve) and let's get started.sudo apt-get install -y clang curl -LO https://go.dev/dl/go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz sudo tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz export PATH=/usr/local/go/bin:$HOME/go/bin:$PATH export CC=clang go install github.com/go-delve/delve/cmd/dlv@latest Writing C code in Go: how?#cgo provides specific syntax we can use to write C code in Go. It has primitives to write pure C code, include statements, build-time flags, reference C code in Go code, and allows us to call Go code from C as well!Consider this program.package main /* #include #include static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" ) func main() { sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) fmt.Println("sum (calculated by C code in Go):", int(sum)) } main.goLet's walk through each element that cgo introduces:import "C": This is used as a signal to the Go build toolchain that this Go file contains foreign C code. It is not an actual package in Go.Preamble: A special comment block immediately preceding import "C". This is where we can write C code that we want to invoke from Go. It can have two different kinds of content:normal C codeC include statementsC references: We can call C functions and types inside Go code as if they are imported from the C package. e.g. C.add(), C.intWe can build this Go package the same way we would any, using go build.$ go build main.go $ ./main sum (calculated by C code in Go): 7 It works! We were able to successfully invoke the C function add from Go's main function and get the correct output. But it's not clear exactly what role cgo plays. Time to dive deeper!cmd/cgo: the build-time utility#go build first identifies if a Go package has any C code in it. If yes, go build invokes cmd/cgo, a command line tool.cmd/cgo parses the C code out of the Go code, invokes the C compiler a few times to understand what each C reference is, its size and alignment (described in a comment in cgo's source) and finally generates pure Go and C files. Finally, go build takes over, compiles the files and links them into the final binary.Let's look at the file generation step in detail.cgo needs to generate pure Go and C files that can be compiled by the Go and C compilers respectively. cgo will substitute all C references with pure Go references and generate bridge code between the Go and C code.For all referenced C types, cgo generates equivalent Go types. For example, cgo generates type _Ctype_int int32 for C.int. In generated Go files, cgo substitutes all references to C.int with _Ctype_int. Running go tool cgo by hand writes these files to an _obj directory.$ go tool cgo main.go $ grep '^type _Ctype_int ' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go type _Ctype_int int32 $ grep '_Ctype_int' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' sum := (_Cfunc_add)(_Ctype_int(3), _Ctype_int(4)) For functions, it is a little more involved since we need to take care of calling conventions. Instead of translating the calling convention between Go and C, which comes with the overhead of dealing with CPU registers and stack locations across different C compilers and CPU architectures, cgo side steps this completely.Go runtime calls a C function of only one shape: a function that takes one pointer argument and returns nothing. It is the one function shape Go's runtime knows how to call on every platform. But in our example, the C function add takes two int arguments and returns an int, so what gives?cgo generates wrapper code in Go and C to bridge this.The original invocation from Go looked like:sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) The generated wrapper Go function looks like this:$ grep -B1 -A7 '^func _Cfunc_add' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go //go:cgo_unsafe_args func _Cfunc_add(p0 _Ctype_int, p1 _Ctype_int) (r1 _Ctype_int) { _cgo_runtime_cgocall(_cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&p0))) if _Cgo_always_false { _Cgo_use(p0) _Cgo_use(p1) } return } //go:cgo_unsafe_args tells the Go compiler to place the arguments and return variables consecutively on the stack instead of the standard register based calling convention. With that, a single pointer can be used to reference the arguments since they are all in consecutive memory, which in this case is &p0._cgo_runtime_cgocall (i.e. runtime.cgocall) takes a pointer to the C function to invoke (which is another wrapper function, here _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add) and a single pointer to where the arguments reside in memory (here &p0). runtime.cgocall does some more nifty things and finally invokes the cross-language call.While the packaged arguments bit is solved for Go, our add function in C still expects 2 arguments and a return value. To handle the C side of this transition, cgo also generates a C wrapper function. For our add function it looks like this:$ grep -B2 -A16 'Cfunc_add(void \*v)' _obj/main.cgo2.c CGO_NO_SANITIZE_THREAD void _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add(void *v) { struct { int p0; int p1; int r; char __pad12[4]; } __attribute__((__packed__)) *_cgo_a = v; char *_cgo_stktop = _cgo_topofstack(); __typeof__(_cgo_a->r) _cgo_r; _cgo_tsan_acquire(); _cgo_r = add(_cgo_a->p0, _cgo_a->p1); _cgo_tsan_release(); _cgo_a = (void*)((char*)_cgo_a + (_cgo_topofstack() - _cgo_stktop)); _cgo_a->r = _cgo_r; _cgo_msan_write(&_cgo_a->r, sizeof(_cgo_a->r)); } This wrapper function resolves the pointer received from the cross-language call into a struct with the C function's input and output values. Then it calls the C function add normally with the arguments and writes the result back into the expected place in memory.Finally, C.add in the generated Go file is replaced with _Cfunc_add, as the sum := line in the first listing showed.At this point, cmd/cgo has generated files which contain pure Go and pure C code. It does some final validation checks and ensures there are no errors. Finally, control is handed back to go build.go build invokes the Go compiler to compile the Go files and the C compiler handles the C files. The result is object files from each compilation which need to be linked together, along with other C libraries if needed. For packages like ours, the C linker handles the linking. In some cases, Go handles linking itself.Afterwards, we have a single binary.Pointer safety checks#In the above example, we were passing scalar arguments from Go to C. But things get a little tricky when we pass pointers across the language boundary.When pointers to memory allocated by Go are passed to C, the garbage collector can no longer track every copy. While Go keeps the memory an argument points to directly, ie top level pointers, safe for the duration of the cgo call, any memory reachable from such a pointer, ie nested pointers, do not get such guarantee. There is also a possibility that C can hold references to Go-owned memory beyond the cgo call.To handle issues like this, Go has two rules for passing memory between Go and C:The memory a Go pointer passed to C points to must not contain an unpinned Go pointer.C must not keep a copy of an unpinned Go pointer beyond the cgo call.Go cannot control what C does, so it's not possible to add checks for the second rule. For the first rule, cgo handles this in two steps: at build time and at runtime.During build time, if cgo cannot rule out the possibility of a nested pointer, it adds a runtime check enforced by the function runtime.cgoCheckPointer. (This check can be disabled by setting GODEBUG=cgocheck=0.)Consider the following example where we pass a double pointer to int from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goLet's see the Go code that cgo generates for this:$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgoBase0 := &s.other _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer(_cgoBase0) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgoBase0, 0 == 0) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() fmt.Println("ok") } The cgo build-time CLI adds a _cgoCheckPointer check for the double pointer argument, &s.other. runtime.cgoCheckPointer is responsible for checking the parameters and panicking if any nested pointer is unpinned. Our current example will panic at runtime:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer It is the programmer's job to make sure the memory backing nested pointers remains safe for the duration of the cgo call. This can be done with runtime.Pinner, ensuring the memory backing the pointer is neither moved nor freed by the garbage collector until it is explicitly unpinned.Modifying the above example, such that s.other is pinned:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "runtime" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} var pinner runtime.Pinner pinner.Pin(s.other) defer pinner.Unpin() C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goGive it a run.$ go run main.go ok This time when runtime.cgoCheckPointer runs, it sees the nested pointer, s.other, is pinned. No panic needed.Sidenote: until Go 1.21 we just couldn't pass C a pointer to memory containing Go pointers at all. Go 1.21 is when runtime.Pinner was released.But cgo does these transformations at the syntax level without knowledge of the Go types of the arguments. This has some interesting ramifications.Panicking on legal code#cgo can only handle and transform very simple patterns in syntax. And when it can't handle a pattern things get weird.Consider the following example where we are passing a pointer to a byte array from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) // passes } main.goIn this program, cgo saw the pointer to the byte array, &s.small, directly being passed to the C function. The check will look only at the memory of the byte array, s.small, and see it contains no pointers. This matches the docs: when passing a pointer to a field in a struct, "the Go memory in question is the memory occupied by the field, not the entire struct." It builds and runs just fine.$ go run main.go $ echo $? 0 But we can write that same exact program with a pattern cgo can not handle: assigning the unsafe pointer to a variable and passing that to C.take.The following example has only one change, instead of invoking the C function with unsafe.Pointer(&s.small), the argument is a variable holding the unsafe pointer:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) C.take(p) // panics } main.goGiving it a run, we see that it panics.$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer That's weird! Let's print out the addresses we're operating on to prove they're really the address of s.small.package main /* #include static void take(void *p) { printf("C got %p\n", p); fflush(stdout); } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} fmt.Printf("s %p\n", s) fmt.Printf("&s.small %p\n", &s.small) C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) fmt.Printf("p %p\n", p) C.take(p) } main.goRunning it, we see both the arguments have the same address:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -5 s 0x2fbb87ede080 &s.small 0x2fbb87ede088 C got 0x2fbb87ede088 p 0x2fbb87ede088 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer So we're definitely looking at the same address the whole time. Why on earth is the program panicking with the variable and successfully executing when passing the pointer directly?Let's look at the traceback to find out where is the panic coming from:$ go build -o demo main.go $ GOTRACEBACK=system ./demo 2>&1 | sed -n '/^panic:/,/^$/p;/^goroutine 1 /,/^$/p' panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer goroutine 1 gp=0x34af3ed561e0 m=0 mp=0x57d3e0 [running]: panic({0x5629f8?, 0x34af3ee1a030?}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/panic.go:878 +0x159 fp=0x34af3ed9dd18 sp=0x34af3ed9dc70 pc=0x47b7b9 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer(0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:773 +0x12a fp=0x34af3ed9dd88 sp=0x34af3ed9dd18 pc=0x414eea runtime.cgoCheckArg(0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0?, 0x1, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:750 +0x25c fp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 sp=0x34af3ed9dd88 pc=0x414b1c runtime.cgoCheckPointer({0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028}, {0x0, 0x0}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:626 +0x146 fp=0x34af3ed9de30 sp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 pc=0x47a1c6 main.main.func2(...) /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 main.main() /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 +0x185 fp=0x34af3ed9deb8 sp=0x34af3ed9de30 pc=0x49e785 runtime.main() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/proc.go:302 +0x427 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 sp=0x34af3ed9deb8 pc=0x44a187 runtime.goexit({}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/asm_amd64.s:1264 +0x1 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe8 sp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 pc=0x481341 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer panics. This function is called when the runtime does not know the type of the memory that the pointer points to. It finds the full heap object containing the given pointer and validates that no unpinned pointers exist in the object slots. In our example, that means no unpinned pointer should exist in the whole object s, not just the field s.small.Following the execution with delve, we can see the above in action:$ go build -gcflags="all=-N -l" -o demo main.go Type 'help' for list of commands. (dlv) break runtime/cgocall.go:771 Breakpoint 1 set at 0x419609 for runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (dlv) c s 0x3427e8302290 &s.small 0x3427e8302298 C got 0x3427e8302298 p 0x3427e8302298 > [Breakpoint 1] runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (hits goroutine(1):1 total:1) (PC: 0x419609) Warning: debugging optimized function 766: for { 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } => 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return (dlv) print p unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302298) (dlv) print span.elemsize 16 (dlv) print unsafe.Pointer(addr) unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302290) (dlv) next > runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:772 (PC: 0x419611) Warning: debugging optimized function 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) => 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return 777: } (dlv) print pp unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e831e008) (dlv) frame 4 print s.other (*int)(0x3427e831e008) *0 Basically, when cgo doesn't recognize how a pointer argument was written, it tells the runtime nothing about what the pointer refers to. In such cases, runtime expects all pointers in the base object to be pinned. Even though the code had nothing to do with s.other, even though the C code doesn't use this whatsoever, the runtime didn't have enough information to know that and panics conservatively. But also wrongly.Even parentheses obstruct the pattern matching:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer((&s.small))) } main.go$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer((&s.small)) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgo0, nil) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() } $ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer This has been a problem in Go for a decade: golang/go#15318 and golang/go#18184 (both 2016, each closed as a duplicate), the gzip Write example in golang/go#28606 (2018, open), and golang/go#70274 (2024, closed as a duplicate), where wrapping the argument in parentheses is enough to cause the panic.In the first issue, maintainer Ian Lance Taylor called this "a known deficiency in the current cgo pointer checker." But the docs never tell you to take the address inside the call, and he explained why in 2016: "there is no intent that that be a permanent requirement. The intent is what you quote from the docs: the memory in question is the memory occupied by the field." By 2024 he wrote of a related case: "I don't know how to fix this except to do full type checking on the cgo input file, which is difficult as we currently expect the type checker to run on cgo output, not cgo input."Real-world projects have run into this too. Wails panicked on macOS because a buffer pointer was assigned to a variable before the C call. Envoy's Go extensions pass pointers that do break the rule, and its Go cluster specifier just makes everyone disable cgocheck.But let's pause and also look at what's going on here from a performance perspective.Making checks extremely expensive#If Go is checking every pointer in an object, what happens as we grow the number of pointers to check? Let's create three structs with increasingly larger arrays of pointers. We'll pass a field from the struct (with and without type info) to a C function.package ptrcost /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S1 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [1 << 10]*int } type S4 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [4 << 10]*int } type S16 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [16 << 10]*int } func inCall1(s *S1) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall4(s *S4) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall16(s *S16) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func viaVar1(s *S1) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar4(s *S4) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar16(s *S16) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } ptrcost.goAnd let's write a little benchmark wrapper.package ptrcost import "testing" func BenchmarkInCall1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall1(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall4(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall16(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar1(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar4(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar16(s) } } ptrcost_test.goLet's try it out.$ go test -c -o ptr.test ptrcost.go ptrcost_test.go $ ./ptr.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime 200ms goos: linux goarch: amd64 cpu: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8280 CPU @ 2.70GHz BenchmarkInCall1x-2 4633052 48.34 ns/op BenchmarkInCall4x-2 4899542 48.43 ns/op BenchmarkInCall16x-2 4904744 48.26 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar1x-2 45789 5241 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar4x-2 10000 22389 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar16x-2 3044 75748 ns/op PASS The cost stays constant even with an increasing number of pointers when passing with type info. But the cost grows linearly with the number of fields to check when passing without type info. Lack of type info, in the above case, incurs between 110x to about 1600x performance cost.The expense of checking objects full of pointers has been known since 2016.Checking only two levels deep#While the pointer checks are exhaustive in the array case, Go does not exhaustively check nested structures.We can demonstrate this with a program that builds a linked list of N nodes, pins some of the nodes after the head, and passes &head.next to a C function that walks the list.package main /* struct node { struct node *next; }; static long walk(void *p) { long n = 0; for (struct node *nd = *(struct node **)p; nd; nd = nd->next) n++; return n; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "os" "runtime" "strconv" "unsafe" ) type node struct { next *node } func main() { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[1]) // nodes in the list pinned, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[2]) // nodes pinned after the head var pinner runtime.Pinner defer pinner.Unpin() head := &node{} cur := head for i := 1; i < n; i++ { cur.next = &node{} cur = cur.next if i <= pinned { pinner.Pin(cur) } } walked := C.walk(unsafe.Pointer(&head.next)) fmt.Println("C walked", walked, "nodes") } main.go$ go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 2 1 C walked 1 nodes $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 2 C walked 2 nodes $ ./list 1000000 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes The pointer we pass, &head.next, points at memory holding a pointer to node 2, so node 2 must be pinned. The check then scans node 2's object and finds node 3, so node 3 must be pinned too. But it doesn't go any further.In the last run, C reads 999,997 nodes that aren't pinned, which the docs forbid: "Go memory reachable from these function arguments must be pinned as long as the C code has access to it."Even cgocheck2, which the docs say does "complete checking", does not catch this:$ GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes So we went from expensively exhaustive on the array of pointers example to cheap on the deeply nested pointer example.Parting thoughts#These examples are not exhaustive. Ian Lance Taylor has said he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go issues for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

Grab dependencies (clang, Go 1.27.0 and Go debugger, delve) and let's get started.sudo apt-get install -y clang curl -LO https://go.dev/dl/go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz sudo tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz export PATH=/usr/local/go/bin:$HOME/go/bin:$PATH export CC=clang go install github.com/go-delve/delve/cmd/dlv@latest Writing C code in Go: how?#cgo provides specific syntax we can use to write C code in Go. It has primitives to write pure C code, include statements, build-time flags, reference C code in Go code, and allows us to call Go code from C as well!Consider this program.package main /* #include #include static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" ) func main() { sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) fmt.Println("sum (calculated by C code in Go):", int(sum)) } main.goLet's walk through each element that cgo introduces:import "C": This is used as a signal to the Go build toolchain that this Go file contains foreign C code. It is not an actual package in Go.Preamble: A special comment block immediately preceding import "C". This is where we can write C code that we want to invoke from Go. It can have two different kinds of content:normal C codeC include statementsC references: We can call C functions and types inside Go code as if they are imported from the C package. e.g. C.add(), C.intWe can build this Go package the same way we would any, using go build.$ go build main.go $ ./main sum (calculated by C code in Go): 7 It works! We were able to successfully invoke the C function add from Go's main function and get the correct output. But it's not clear exactly what role cgo plays. Time to dive deeper!cmd/cgo: the build-time utility#go build first identifies if a Go package has any C code in it. If yes, go build invokes cmd/cgo, a command line tool.cmd/cgo parses the C code out of the Go code, invokes the C compiler a few times to understand what each C reference is, its size and alignment (described in a comment in cgo's source) and finally generates pure Go and C files. Finally, go build takes over, compiles the files and links them into the final binary.Let's look at the file generation step in detail.cgo needs to generate pure Go and C files that can be compiled by the Go and C compilers respectively. cgo will substitute all C references with pure Go references and generate bridge code between the Go and C code.For all referenced C types, cgo generates equivalent Go types. For example, cgo generates type _Ctype_int int32 for C.int. In generated Go files, cgo substitutes all references to C.int with _Ctype_int. Running go tool cgo by hand writes these files to an _obj directory.$ go tool cgo main.go $ grep '^type _Ctype_int ' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go type _Ctype_int int32 $ grep '_Ctype_int' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' sum := (_Cfunc_add)(_Ctype_int(3), _Ctype_int(4)) For functions, it is a little more involved since we need to take care of calling conventions. Instead of translating the calling convention between Go and C, which comes with the overhead of dealing with CPU registers and stack locations across different C compilers and CPU architectures, cgo side steps this completely.Go runtime calls a C function of only one shape: a function that takes one pointer argument and returns nothing. It is the one function shape Go's runtime knows how to call on every platform. But in our example, the C function add takes two int arguments and returns an int, so what gives?cgo generates wrapper code in Go and C to bridge this.The original invocation from Go looked like:sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) The generated wrapper Go function looks like this:$ grep -B1 -A7 '^func _Cfunc_add' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go //go:cgo_unsafe_args func _Cfunc_add(p0 _Ctype_int, p1 _Ctype_int) (r1 _Ctype_int) { _cgo_runtime_cgocall(_cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&p0))) if _Cgo_always_false { _Cgo_use(p0) _Cgo_use(p1) } return } //go:cgo_unsafe_args tells the Go compiler to place the arguments and return variables consecutively on the stack instead of the standard register based calling convention. With that, a single pointer can be used to reference the arguments since they are all in consecutive memory, which in this case is &p0._cgo_runtime_cgocall (i.e. runtime.cgocall) takes a pointer to the C function to invoke (which is another wrapper function, here _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add) and a single pointer to where the arguments reside in memory (here &p0). runtime.cgocall does some more nifty things and finally invokes the cross-language call.While the packaged arguments bit is solved for Go, our add function in C still expects 2 arguments and a return value. To handle the C side of this transition, cgo also generates a C wrapper function. For our add function it looks like this:$ grep -B2 -A16 'Cfunc_add(void \*v)' _obj/main.cgo2.c CGO_NO_SANITIZE_THREAD void _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add(void *v) { struct { int p0; int p1; int r; char __pad12[4]; } __attribute__((__packed__)) *_cgo_a = v; char *_cgo_stktop = _cgo_topofstack(); __typeof__(_cgo_a->r) _cgo_r; _cgo_tsan_acquire(); _cgo_r = add(_cgo_a->p0, _cgo_a->p1); _cgo_tsan_release(); _cgo_a = (void*)((char*)_cgo_a + (_cgo_topofstack() - _cgo_stktop)); _cgo_a->r = _cgo_r; _cgo_msan_write(&_cgo_a->r, sizeof(_cgo_a->r)); } This wrapper function resolves the pointer received from the cross-language call into a struct with the C function's input and output values. Then it calls the C function add normally with the arguments and writes the result back into the expected place in memory.Finally, C.add in the generated Go file is replaced with _Cfunc_add, as the sum := line in the first listing showed.At this point, cmd/cgo has generated files which contain pure Go and pure C code. It does some final validation checks and ensures there are no errors. Finally, control is handed back to go build.go build invokes the Go compiler to compile the Go files and the C compiler handles the C files. The result is object files from each compilation which need to be linked together, along with other C libraries if needed. For packages like ours, the C linker handles the linking. In some cases, Go handles linking itself.Afterwards, we have a single binary.Pointer safety checks#In the above example, we were passing scalar arguments from Go to C. But things get a little tricky when we pass pointers across the language boundary.When pointers to memory allocated by Go are passed to C, the garbage collector can no longer track every copy. While Go keeps the memory an argument points to directly, ie top level pointers, safe for the duration of the cgo call, any memory reachable from such a pointer, ie nested pointers, do not get such guarantee. There is also a possibility that C can hold references to Go-owned memory beyond the cgo call.To handle issues like this, Go has two rules for passing memory between Go and C:The memory a Go pointer passed to C points to must not contain an unpinned Go pointer.C must not keep a copy of an unpinned Go pointer beyond the cgo call.Go cannot control what C does, so it's not possible to add checks for the second rule. For the first rule, cgo handles this in two steps: at build time and at runtime.During build time, if cgo cannot rule out the possibility of a nested pointer, it adds a runtime check enforced by the function runtime.cgoCheckPointer. (This check can be disabled by setting GODEBUG=cgocheck=0.)Consider the following example where we pass a double pointer to int from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goLet's see the Go code that cgo generates for this:$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgoBase0 := &s.other _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer(_cgoBase0) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgoBase0, 0 == 0) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() fmt.Println("ok") } The cgo build-time CLI adds a _cgoCheckPointer check for the double pointer argument, &s.other. runtime.cgoCheckPointer is responsible for checking the parameters and panicking if any nested pointer is unpinned. Our current example will panic at runtime:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer It is the programmer's job to make sure the memory backing nested pointers remains safe for the duration of the cgo call. This can be done with runtime.Pinner, ensuring the memory backing the pointer is neither moved nor freed by the garbage collector until it is explicitly unpinned.Modifying the above example, such that s.other is pinned:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "runtime" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} var pinner runtime.Pinner pinner.Pin(s.other) defer pinner.Unpin() C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goGive it a run.$ go run main.go ok This time when runtime.cgoCheckPointer runs, it sees the nested pointer, s.other, is pinned. No panic needed.Sidenote: until Go 1.21 we just couldn't pass C a pointer to memory containing Go pointers at all. Go 1.21 is when runtime.Pinner was released.But cgo does these transformations at the syntax level without knowledge of the Go types of the arguments. This has some interesting ramifications.Panicking on legal code#cgo can only handle and transform very simple patterns in syntax. And when it can't handle a pattern things get weird.Consider the following example where we are passing a pointer to a byte array from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) // passes } main.goIn this program, cgo saw the pointer to the byte array, &s.small, directly being passed to the C function. The check will look only at the memory of the byte array, s.small, and see it contains no pointers. This matches the docs: when passing a pointer to a field in a struct, "the Go memory in question is the memory occupied by the field, not the entire struct." It builds and runs just fine.$ go run main.go $ echo $? 0 But we can write that same exact program with a pattern cgo can not handle: assigning the unsafe pointer to a variable and passing that to C.take.The following example has only one change, instead of invoking the C function with unsafe.Pointer(&s.small), the argument is a variable holding the unsafe pointer:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) C.take(p) // panics } main.goGiving it a run, we see that it panics.$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer That's weird! Let's print out the addresses we're operating on to prove they're really the address of s.small.package main /* #include static void take(void *p) { printf("C got %p\n", p); fflush(stdout); } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} fmt.Printf("s %p\n", s) fmt.Printf("&s.small %p\n", &s.small) C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) fmt.Printf("p %p\n", p) C.take(p) } main.goRunning it, we see both the arguments have the same address:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -5 s 0x2fbb87ede080 &s.small 0x2fbb87ede088 C got 0x2fbb87ede088 p 0x2fbb87ede088 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer So we're definitely looking at the same address the whole time. Why on earth is the program panicking with the variable and successfully executing when passing the pointer directly?Let's look at the traceback to find out where is the panic coming from:$ go build -o demo main.go $ GOTRACEBACK=system ./demo 2>&1 | sed -n '/^panic:/,/^$/p;/^goroutine 1 /,/^$/p' panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer goroutine 1 gp=0x34af3ed561e0 m=0 mp=0x57d3e0 [running]: panic({0x5629f8?, 0x34af3ee1a030?}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/panic.go:878 +0x159 fp=0x34af3ed9dd18 sp=0x34af3ed9dc70 pc=0x47b7b9 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer(0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:773 +0x12a fp=0x34af3ed9dd88 sp=0x34af3ed9dd18 pc=0x414eea runtime.cgoCheckArg(0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0?, 0x1, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:750 +0x25c fp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 sp=0x34af3ed9dd88 pc=0x414b1c runtime.cgoCheckPointer({0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028}, {0x0, 0x0}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:626 +0x146 fp=0x34af3ed9de30 sp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 pc=0x47a1c6 main.main.func2(...) /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 main.main() /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 +0x185 fp=0x34af3ed9deb8 sp=0x34af3ed9de30 pc=0x49e785 runtime.main() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/proc.go:302 +0x427 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 sp=0x34af3ed9deb8 pc=0x44a187 runtime.goexit({}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/asm_amd64.s:1264 +0x1 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe8 sp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 pc=0x481341 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer panics. This function is called when the runtime does not know the type of the memory that the pointer points to. It finds the full heap object containing the given pointer and validates that no unpinned pointers exist in the object slots. In our example, that means no unpinned pointer should exist in the whole object s, not just the field s.small.Following the execution with delve, we can see the above in action:$ go build -gcflags="all=-N -l" -o demo main.go Type 'help' for list of commands. (dlv) break runtime/cgocall.go:771 Breakpoint 1 set at 0x419609 for runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (dlv) c s 0x3427e8302290 &s.small 0x3427e8302298 C got 0x3427e8302298 p 0x3427e8302298 > [Breakpoint 1] runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (hits goroutine(1):1 total:1) (PC: 0x419609) Warning: debugging optimized function 766: for { 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } => 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return (dlv) print p unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302298) (dlv) print span.elemsize 16 (dlv) print unsafe.Pointer(addr) unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302290) (dlv) next > runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:772 (PC: 0x419611) Warning: debugging optimized function 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) => 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return 777: } (dlv) print pp unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e831e008) (dlv) frame 4 print s.other (*int)(0x3427e831e008) *0 Basically, when cgo doesn't recognize how a pointer argument was written, it tells the runtime nothing about what the pointer refers to. In such cases, runtime expects all pointers in the base object to be pinned. Even though the code had nothing to do with s.other, even though the C code doesn't use this whatsoever, the runtime didn't have enough information to know that and panics conservatively. But also wrongly.Even parentheses obstruct the pattern matching:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer((&s.small))) } main.go$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer((&s.small)) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgo0, nil) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() } $ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer This has been a problem in Go for a decade: golang/go#15318 and golang/go#18184 (both 2016, each closed as a duplicate), the gzip Write example in golang/go#28606 (2018, open), and golang/go#70274 (2024, closed as a duplicate), where wrapping the argument in parentheses is enough to cause the panic.In the first issue, maintainer Ian Lance Taylor called this "a known deficiency in the current cgo pointer checker." But the docs never tell you to take the address inside the call, and he explained why in 2016: "there is no intent that that be a permanent requirement. The intent is what you quote from the docs: the memory in question is the memory occupied by the field." By 2024 he wrote of a related case: "I don't know how to fix this except to do full type checking on the cgo input file, which is difficult as we currently expect the type checker to run on cgo output, not cgo input."Real-world projects have run into this too. Wails panicked on macOS because a buffer pointer was assigned to a variable before the C call. Envoy's Go extensions pass pointers that do break the rule, and its Go cluster specifier just makes everyone disable cgocheck.But let's pause and also look at what's going on here from a performance perspective.Making checks extremely expensive#If Go is checking every pointer in an object, what happens as we grow the number of pointers to check? Let's create three structs with increasingly larger arrays of pointers. We'll pass a field from the struct (with and without type info) to a C function.package ptrcost /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S1 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [1 << 10]*int } type S4 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [4 << 10]*int } type S16 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [16 << 10]*int } func inCall1(s *S1) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall4(s *S4) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall16(s *S16) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func viaVar1(s *S1) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar4(s *S4) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar16(s *S16) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } ptrcost.goAnd let's write a little benchmark wrapper.package ptrcost import "testing" func BenchmarkInCall1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall1(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall4(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall16(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar1(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar4(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar16(s) } } ptrcost_test.goLet's try it out.$ go test -c -o ptr.test ptrcost.go ptrcost_test.go $ ./ptr.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime 200ms goos: linux goarch: amd64 cpu: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8280 CPU @ 2.70GHz BenchmarkInCall1x-2 4633052 48.34 ns/op BenchmarkInCall4x-2 4899542 48.43 ns/op BenchmarkInCall16x-2 4904744 48.26 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar1x-2 45789 5241 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar4x-2 10000 22389 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar16x-2 3044 75748 ns/op PASS The cost stays constant even with an increasing number of pointers when passing with type info. But the cost grows linearly with the number of fields to check when passing without type info. Lack of type info, in the above case, incurs between 110x to about 1600x performance cost.The expense of checking objects full of pointers has been known since 2016.Checking only two levels deep#While the pointer checks are exhaustive in the array case, Go does not exhaustively check nested structures.We can demonstrate this with a program that builds a linked list of N nodes, pins some of the nodes after the head, and passes &head.next to a C function that walks the list.package main /* struct node { struct node *next; }; static long walk(void *p) { long n = 0; for (struct node *nd = *(struct node **)p; nd; nd = nd->next) n++; return n; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "os" "runtime" "strconv" "unsafe" ) type node struct { next *node } func main() { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[1]) // nodes in the list pinned, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[2]) // nodes pinned after the head var pinner runtime.Pinner defer pinner.Unpin() head := &node{} cur := head for i := 1; i < n; i++ { cur.next = &node{} cur = cur.next if i <= pinned { pinner.Pin(cur) } } walked := C.walk(unsafe.Pointer(&head.next)) fmt.Println("C walked", walked, "nodes") } main.go$ go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 2 1 C walked 1 nodes $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 2 C walked 2 nodes $ ./list 1000000 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes The pointer we pass, &head.next, points at memory holding a pointer to node 2, so node 2 must be pinned. The check then scans node 2's object and finds node 3, so node 3 must be pinned too. But it doesn't go any further.In the last run, C reads 999,997 nodes that aren't pinned, which the docs forbid: "Go memory reachable from these function arguments must be pinned as long as the C code has access to it."Even cgocheck2, which the docs say does "complete checking", does not catch this:$ GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes So we went from expensively exhaustive on the array of pointers example to cheap on the deeply nested pointer example.Parting thoughts#These examples are not exhaustive. Ian Lance Taylor has said he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go issues for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

cgo provides specific syntax we can use to write C code in Go. It has primitives to write pure C code, include statements, build-time flags, reference C code in Go code, and allows us to call Go code from C as well!Consider this program.package main /* #include #include static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" ) func main() { sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) fmt.Println("sum (calculated by C code in Go):", int(sum)) } main.goLet's walk through each element that cgo introduces:import "C": This is used as a signal to the Go build toolchain that this Go file contains foreign C code. It is not an actual package in Go.Preamble: A special comment block immediately preceding import "C". This is where we can write C code that we want to invoke from Go. It can have two different kinds of content:normal C codeC include statementsC references: We can call C functions and types inside Go code as if they are imported from the C package. e.g. C.add(), C.intWe can build this Go package the same way we would any, using go build.$ go build main.go $ ./main sum (calculated by C code in Go): 7 It works! We were able to successfully invoke the C function add from Go's main function and get the correct output. But it's not clear exactly what role cgo plays. Time to dive deeper!cmd/cgo: the build-time utility#go build first identifies if a Go package has any C code in it. If yes, go build invokes cmd/cgo, a command line tool.cmd/cgo parses the C code out of the Go code, invokes the C compiler a few times to understand what each C reference is, its size and alignment (described in a comment in cgo's source) and finally generates pure Go and C files. Finally, go build takes over, compiles the files and links them into the final binary.Let's look at the file generation step in detail.cgo needs to generate pure Go and C files that can be compiled by the Go and C compilers respectively. cgo will substitute all C references with pure Go references and generate bridge code between the Go and C code.For all referenced C types, cgo generates equivalent Go types. For example, cgo generates type _Ctype_int int32 for C.int. In generated Go files, cgo substitutes all references to C.int with _Ctype_int. Running go tool cgo by hand writes these files to an _obj directory.$ go tool cgo main.go $ grep '^type _Ctype_int ' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go type _Ctype_int int32 $ grep '_Ctype_int' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' sum := (_Cfunc_add)(_Ctype_int(3), _Ctype_int(4)) For functions, it is a little more involved since we need to take care of calling conventions. Instead of translating the calling convention between Go and C, which comes with the overhead of dealing with CPU registers and stack locations across different C compilers and CPU architectures, cgo side steps this completely.Go runtime calls a C function of only one shape: a function that takes one pointer argument and returns nothing. It is the one function shape Go's runtime knows how to call on every platform. But in our example, the C function add takes two int arguments and returns an int, so what gives?cgo generates wrapper code in Go and C to bridge this.The original invocation from Go looked like:sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) The generated wrapper Go function looks like this:$ grep -B1 -A7 '^func _Cfunc_add' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go //go:cgo_unsafe_args func _Cfunc_add(p0 _Ctype_int, p1 _Ctype_int) (r1 _Ctype_int) { _cgo_runtime_cgocall(_cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&p0))) if _Cgo_always_false { _Cgo_use(p0) _Cgo_use(p1) } return } //go:cgo_unsafe_args tells the Go compiler to place the arguments and return variables consecutively on the stack instead of the standard register based calling convention. With that, a single pointer can be used to reference the arguments since they are all in consecutive memory, which in this case is &p0._cgo_runtime_cgocall (i.e. runtime.cgocall) takes a pointer to the C function to invoke (which is another wrapper function, here _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add) and a single pointer to where the arguments reside in memory (here &p0). runtime.cgocall does some more nifty things and finally invokes the cross-language call.While the packaged arguments bit is solved for Go, our add function in C still expects 2 arguments and a return value. To handle the C side of this transition, cgo also generates a C wrapper function. For our add function it looks like this:$ grep -B2 -A16 'Cfunc_add(void \*v)' _obj/main.cgo2.c CGO_NO_SANITIZE_THREAD void _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add(void *v) { struct { int p0; int p1; int r; char __pad12[4]; } __attribute__((__packed__)) *_cgo_a = v; char *_cgo_stktop = _cgo_topofstack(); __typeof__(_cgo_a->r) _cgo_r; _cgo_tsan_acquire(); _cgo_r = add(_cgo_a->p0, _cgo_a->p1); _cgo_tsan_release(); _cgo_a = (void*)((char*)_cgo_a + (_cgo_topofstack() - _cgo_stktop)); _cgo_a->r = _cgo_r; _cgo_msan_write(&_cgo_a->r, sizeof(_cgo_a->r)); } This wrapper function resolves the pointer received from the cross-language call into a struct with the C function's input and output values. Then it calls the C function add normally with the arguments and writes the result back into the expected place in memory.Finally, C.add in the generated Go file is replaced with _Cfunc_add, as the sum := line in the first listing showed.At this point, cmd/cgo has generated files which contain pure Go and pure C code. It does some final validation checks and ensures there are no errors. Finally, control is handed back to go build.go build invokes the Go compiler to compile the Go files and the C compiler handles the C files. The result is object files from each compilation which need to be linked together, along with other C libraries if needed. For packages like ours, the C linker handles the linking. In some cases, Go handles linking itself.Afterwards, we have a single binary.Pointer safety checks#In the above example, we were passing scalar arguments from Go to C. But things get a little tricky when we pass pointers across the language boundary.When pointers to memory allocated by Go are passed to C, the garbage collector can no longer track every copy. While Go keeps the memory an argument points to directly, ie top level pointers, safe for the duration of the cgo call, any memory reachable from such a pointer, ie nested pointers, do not get such guarantee. There is also a possibility that C can hold references to Go-owned memory beyond the cgo call.To handle issues like this, Go has two rules for passing memory between Go and C:The memory a Go pointer passed to C points to must not contain an unpinned Go pointer.C must not keep a copy of an unpinned Go pointer beyond the cgo call.Go cannot control what C does, so it's not possible to add checks for the second rule. For the first rule, cgo handles this in two steps: at build time and at runtime.During build time, if cgo cannot rule out the possibility of a nested pointer, it adds a runtime check enforced by the function runtime.cgoCheckPointer. (This check can be disabled by setting GODEBUG=cgocheck=0.)Consider the following example where we pass a double pointer to int from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goLet's see the Go code that cgo generates for this:$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgoBase0 := &s.other _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer(_cgoBase0) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgoBase0, 0 == 0) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() fmt.Println("ok") } The cgo build-time CLI adds a _cgoCheckPointer check for the double pointer argument, &s.other. runtime.cgoCheckPointer is responsible for checking the parameters and panicking if any nested pointer is unpinned. Our current example will panic at runtime:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer It is the programmer's job to make sure the memory backing nested pointers remains safe for the duration of the cgo call. This can be done with runtime.Pinner, ensuring the memory backing the pointer is neither moved nor freed by the garbage collector until it is explicitly unpinned.Modifying the above example, such that s.other is pinned:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "runtime" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} var pinner runtime.Pinner pinner.Pin(s.other) defer pinner.Unpin() C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goGive it a run.$ go run main.go ok This time when runtime.cgoCheckPointer runs, it sees the nested pointer, s.other, is pinned. No panic needed.Sidenote: until Go 1.21 we just couldn't pass C a pointer to memory containing Go pointers at all. Go 1.21 is when runtime.Pinner was released.But cgo does these transformations at the syntax level without knowledge of the Go types of the arguments.
